utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-5/18-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. Karadzic, are you in good spirits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As ever, thank you, Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to address myself first of all to the Prosecution today, so I shall ask for appearances on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, Katrina Gustafson, and case manager Iain Reid for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first issue that I want to address, Mr. Tieger, is disclosure. The Trial Chamber issued a decision on the 27th of April in relation to a motion on the modalities of Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure, and at that stage the Prosecution were content to adopt a method which was more or less that sought by the accused. However, it had to be put into effect. Has that been done?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are actually on track in relation to disclosure on external hard drive. This will all be done in time, and we are confident that we will meet the 7 May disclosure dead-line except for one item that is actually currently an issue, a technical issue, mostly, and that's the disclosure of audio files. And we have actually provided a notification on the difficulties that we are encountering in this respect, and we filed it yesterday. And we will not be able to provide all the audio files by 7 May. That's technically not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unlike you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm unable to understand entirely how this difficulty has arisen. Can you help me a little more in explaining what the work is that needs to be done and why these files are not capable of instant reproduction for use by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have filed the details actually in our notification, and the problem is that those things need to be transferred first from the Registrar to the Prosecutor's office and then they need to be technically processed. And as it is mentioned in the submission, it takes per days file -- audio file, it takes at least 20 to 30 minutes and often several hours when the files are corrupted. And we have explained that the pace is just not that fast as it can be -- so that we can meet the 7th of May. If you want to have some more real technical details, Mr. Iain is actually, our case manager, dealing with these problems, and he is definitely better-placed than myself to go into the technical details. I thought that what we had provided was actually sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your notification you refer to 15 to 20 per cent of the audio files having been found to be corrupted. These ones, are they digital files or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So am I understanding the problem correctly in that normally these would be very quickly reproduced, but because of corruption you have to go back to the original which is an analogue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Reid can better explain it, instead of telling first me and then I tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your moment of glory, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. REID
utterances.text: When the audio-visual department uses a special programme that they use to process the audio from the various booths, it's called FTR, and when one of these sets of audio from a day's session is found to be corrupted, they have to go back to the original digital tapes, and they then have to record the audio coming off of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So everything is digital, but it just takes longer because of corruption, basically?

utterances.speaker: MR. REID
utterances.text: Yeah, because it's from a tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is there anything else you want to say on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. In relation to disclosure everything else is on track. There's actually nothing to mention in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is the extended date that you seek in relation to these audio files?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: End of June, Your Honour, 30 of June to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, there are two issues here. There is the question of Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure in general, and that's the disclosure of witness statements, and the Prosecution appear to be doing that in cooperation with the Registry by the means that you asked them to do it. So can I take it that in general this form of disclosure is working satisfactorily?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to thank the Trial Chamber and Your Lordship for appointing Mr. Sladojevic so that now my team can be complete; it will be complete within ten days. And I'd also like to thank Ms. Davidson for sending me the agenda in advance of the conference. That will help me a great deal, and it will help even more if I'm provided it earlier on. I'd also like to congratulate the Roma and the Serbs on St. George's day which it is today and to ask him not hold it against us for working during St. George's day. St. George's day protects the English, and I assume the Scots as well, I don't believe he's against the Scots, so we seem to be holding all these status conferences during Serb feast days and holidays. Now as far as disclosure is concerned, I don't oppose extending the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. Karadzic, I'm shocked to hear your sympathy for St. George, but I understand it nevertheless. He's not a protector of the Scots, so he is not one that you can particularly invoke in this exchange with me. However, please get on to disclosure. And in case it is of interest to you, it is to St. Andrew to whom I turn, rather than St. George.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm glad to hear that. I know St. Andrew the First-Called, and I know that the Irish have Patrick, and the English have St. George, and St. George is much celebrated among our people. Now, as far as disclosure is concerned, I'm not opposed to giving an extension of time to the Prosecutor, as much time as they need, and I would be even less opposed to that had I been able to defend myself while at liberty. But I don't oppose it anyway in detention. But what I want to say is something else. In light of the decision made by the Trial Chamber about my knowledge of the language - and this is something I complained about - and if, Your Lordship, you take a look at the situation, you'll see that I have to listen to 600-odd days of testimony for me to be able to understand it all, which means that I'll need at least 300 days. Now they need a lot of time to tape all this, but that's much easier because it's a technical matter, whereas I have to go through all the material, to understand it, and to prepare my Defence on the basis of 550 days of testimony instead of it being provided to me in the Serbian language and in transcript form. And I'd like to raise some other difficulties later on in due course that stem from the position of the OTP and its conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I take that as no objection being stated to the requested extension of time for disclosure of the audio-tapes. I take it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, they are being disclosed systematically as they are translated rather than held back for disclosure in one batch at the end?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue actually is here with the external hard drive. We are actually producing this onto the external hard drive, and once it is completed then we provide this external hard drive. It's not that we can now do it piecemeal, at least that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's plainly not going to be satisfactory. An extension to the 30th of June for all disclosure of these tapes is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it seems to me possible - and Mr. Reid has just confirmed that - that we can provide the external hard drive with the -- tomorrow with the materials that have been produced to date and thereafter provide the completed tapes on DVD seriatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. Well, on that basis the Chamber is minded to grant your request but to urge you to disclose material as soon as it is complete in a form that can be transferred to the accused, so that means regular disclosure during the period up until the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour. It was a misunderstanding of the technicals involved on my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I read into what you've said so far, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that the disclosure of expert witness material is also on track. The dates differ for some, but can I take it that that will be completed according to the anticipated schedule?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to turn to certain of the motions which are currently before the Trial Chamber to see if we can speedily resolve the issues that arise from these. And the first of these that I wish to address is the motion challenging the form of the indictment relating to averments about joint criminal enterprises. And these averments assert the involvement of the accused in four separate joint criminal enterprises, but the averments assert also that the first of these is an overarching joint criminal enterprise. That would tend to indicate that the other three somehow or other fall within the ambit of this overarching joint criminal enterprise, but a closer reading of the indictment indicates that the third and fourth do not on the face of the indictment appear to fall within the overarching joint criminal enterprise, albeit they are said to be related to it. Now, that would appear to be the effect of a reading of the indictment in light of this challenge. Mr. Tieger, can you assist me in clarifying that that is in fact what is intended in these averments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With some modification, I believe, Your Honour. I appreciate the opportunity both to clarify this issue with the Court and with respect to the Defence pleadings. In particular, I noted that the Defence pleading asserted in one of its paragraphs that - and I can find that shortly - that the objectives as stated in paragraph 8 of the indictment of the four joint criminal enterprises were identical. And I think it's important to clarify that. If the Court turns to paragraph 8 of the indictment, it identifies the -- after describing and articulating the overarching joint criminal enterprise, it specifies the objectives of the three additional joint criminal enterprises, modes of the liability for the crimes alleged as -- and they are articulated there: The terror campaign in Sarajevo, the elimination of Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, and the taking of UN personnel as hostages, articulating further that the pursuit of these objectives, the objectives of these discrete joint criminal enterprises alleged, was related to the objective of the overarching joint criminal enterprise, to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims. And that, Your Honour, is further clarified in the interim pre-trial brief, where there -- where we note the further -- the relationship between the four joint criminal enterprises, identifying again the distinction between the objectives alleged, but further indicating that each of the discrete JCEs furthered the -- was related to and furthered the objective of the overarching of JCE. So I think it's fair to say that the distinctions noted by the Court and the similarities noted by the Court are accurate. With respect to the Srebrenica JCE as the Court noted, and I think that's what it was referring to, we have alleged that it emerged from and clearly advanced the overarching JCE, but again these are alleged as separate and discrete objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you look at paragraphs 9 and 10 of the indictment following the one you've just referred to, they seem to encompass only, so far as Srebrenica is concerned, the Counts 2 to 8. Now, they don't seem to encompass 9 and 10, which relate to the -- also to the Srebrenica allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake, Mr. Tieger. The allegations in paragraph 9 and 10 do not appear to relate to the campaign of terror in Sarajevo, nor to the taking of hostages. So these are Counts 9, 10, and 11 of the indictment, and therefore it's difficult to see how the initial joint criminal enterprise can be said to be overarching.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- perhaps there's a misunderstanding in the sense of the term "overarching." It was certainly not intended to suggest the existence of a single JCE. The sense of "overarching" is the sense as described further in the interim pre-trial brief, and that is that the -- during the course of this lengthy conduct -- criminal campaign from 1992 to 1995, for the purposes identified both in the interim pre-trial brief and in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but does that mean "overarching" is meaningless here and should be deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think in fairness it signalled the relationship between the discrete JCEs and -- it seems to me that if they were just alleged without benefit of that term, they would misleadingly signal to the Court and to the accused that they were four individual, discrete, unrelated JCEs. And the use of the term "overarching" provides greater clarity and understanding about the relationship between the four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take as an example to try to clarify this, what is the relationship between the so-called overarching joint criminal enterprise and the joint criminal enterprise to take UN peacekeepers as hostages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as we indicated in the interim pre-trial brief, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let's look -- the indictment surely has got to tell the accused what the relationship between two joint criminal enterprises is. You can't seriously be maintaining that it's good enough to do that in the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think there -- the jurisprudence provides for amplification in the -- by way of the pre-trial brief, but having said that it seems to me the relationship is pretty clear. The effort -- the taking of hostages was in order to forestall air-strikes, to maintain the strength of the Bosnian Serb military machine, and therefore to preserve the ability to advance the objectives of the overarching JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And yet you don't say it's just part of the initial JCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we say it more clearly, Your Honour. We identify the -- we -- the whole point of the JCE is not -- and if I may, I don't think the Court is suffering from this misconception, but it's clear to me that the accused in his motion was, and that was the articulation of JCEs as separate charges, which they are not. JCE is a mode of liability which explains the relationship between the accused and the crimes alleged, and by focus -- and the accused under his rationale, as expressed in his motion, presumably had no difficulty with the manner in which the first indictment was alleged. This indictment, however, by focusing more carefully and narrowly and on the specific people involved, the specific times involved, the specific events involved provides heightened clarity about the accused's responsibility for the underlying crimes. Underlying crimes remain the same, but now the accused and the Court are focused much more clearly on the specific events, people, times, and locations which give rise to that liability. And that's the impact of the separate JCEs, and that's the benefit of the charging of separate JCEs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me what "overarching" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It means that -- well, first of all, it -- I think it refers to both the temporal period and the objective. And that means that during the entire period of time encompassed by all four JCEs, the -- the overarching JCE is the one that was in place for that period of time. And further, the objective of that JCE was related to and furthered by the discretely alleged other three JCEs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just I think perhaps the last point I would like you to clarify for me at the moment is: Where is it you make clear the relationship between the joint criminal enterprise to produce terror in Sarajevo and the so-called overarching joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in the same sense that I described before, Your Honour, I believe in paragraphs 6 through 8 is where the relationship between the JCEs is described. And again, as I indicated before, in paragraph 8 the indictment avers that the pursuit of those objectives - and in Sarajevo the objective was to spread terror, as the Court has indicated - was related to the objective of the overarching of JCE. And again that is amplified further in the pre-trial brief, but I would also say that the relationship between striking terror in a population and the effort to permanently remove a population is -- should not be a difficult one to grasp on the face of the indictment itself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why it's quite difficult to understand why you separate it from the overarching -- the so-called overarching. But it seems such an obvious way of trying to remove the population, but you don't say that that was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we say in -- and again, I gather the Court is somewhat reluctant to have me refer to representations in the pre-trial brief, but I -- I -- since I'm going to say that in any event I might as well refer to where it's previously articulated, and we identify a number of the motives behind the terror campaign, including the effort to secure concessions from the Bosnian government and the international community, the interest in exacting revenge, the interest in securing concessions in negotiations to cement gains and to obtain a resolution consistent with the objectives of the Bosnian Serbs, and more generally to secure and cement the objectives of the overarching JCE. So the -- again, we're dealing with a mode of liability which deals with different people in a specified location over a specified period of time for a variety of purposes. And the -- it seems to have greater focus and greater clarity for the Court to focus on the allegation that there was a campaign of terror rather than -- which had a number of motives as alleged, a number of purposes, at different times and advanced different specific purposes, all of which were related to the overarching JCE. So to the extent it's unnecessary at any given time and for any given -- with any given witness to link it up to the JCE, the trial process is advanced. And furthermore, should -- I think we -- the immediate purpose of the terror campaign, the immediate objective as we've alleged, was not to physically remove portions of the Sarajevo population; it was instead to inflict terror on a besieged population. And that is a different objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, it is further complicated, as you know, by the fact that the murders in Sarajevo are actually encompassed under the overarching joint criminal enterprise, but that's deliberately done, is it, in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the case, Your Honour. I mean, there are -- the -- there is an aspect in which the Sarajevo municipalities are related to the -- there's part of the overarching campaign was to physically remove people from Sarajevo, but have to -- yeah, I'd refer the Court to paragraph 65: "The acts of murder that form part of the objective to spread terror among the civilian population of Sarajevo through a campaign of sniping and shelling were carried out between April 1992 and November 1995 by members of the Sarajevo forces; they include the deaths caused by sniping and shelling described in Schedule F and Schedule G."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but these are Counts 4, 5, and 6 which are said to fall under the overarching joint criminal enterprise, and therefore would appear to encompass the killings in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's ... Sorry, Your Honour, if I could have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that those -- it's -- I think it's accurate to say that they include the overarching JCE, but they are -- they are a reflection of the -- they include all of the JCEs, and because the JCEs are modes of liability, and the modes of liability leading to the establishing responsibility for the crimes that are alleged in those counts. So it's -- they don't fall exclusively under the overarching JCE, but they encompass all of the committing modes of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's just a lot of words to me, Mr. Tieger. This whole exercise is designed to identify what crimes were committed in what circumstances, and the circumstances include the mode by which liability rests with the accused. In other words, the mode of his involvement in the commission, ordering or otherwise, in relation to these crimes. Now, my understanding of this indictment is that the first eight counts are said to fall under the first joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's wrong, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I mean, the counts, Counts 4, 5, and 6 is extermination and murder, for example, embrace all of the modes of liability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- giving rise to those charges, including the three JCEs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the only two counts that are exclusive, Your Honour, would be Count 2, Srebrenica; Count 11, hostages; and maybe -- and 9 and 10 relating to Sarajevo. So 9 and 10 is the terror count exclusively; 2 is Srebrenica; and 11 is the taking of hostages. The others are the underlying crimes which emerge from the various modes of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you look at paragraph 9 again then, please. And this is relating to the overarching joint criminal enterprise. Now, it's Count 1 that's included there; Count 2 is not; and persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and forcible transfer are included. And then Count 2 falls in as a possible JCE 3, I think. Am I misunderstanding paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it comes in on a different basis into the overarching joint criminal enterprise. But on the face of it, that joint criminal enterprise appears to cover the murder and extermination counts which include Sarajevo. Now, what this comes to at the end of the day, Mr. Tieger, is, it would appear, a lack of clarity in the indictment in relation to the subject of the connection between the joint criminal enterprises, inter se, and the connection between these various joint criminal enterprises as modes of liability and the crimes to which they relate. And that is an issue on which the Chamber will issue a decision very shortly, and I just want to ensure that you've had an opportunity to make whatever submissions you wish before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, Your Honour. If I may, I -- frankly, now that I have some understanding of the Court's concern, and I'll be frank and say I didn't grasp that that was the nature of the Court's concern from the messages we received before, I would like an opportunity to further clarify it. And I'm grateful for the Court's desire to ensure we do have an opportunity to make those submissions before the Court makes a ruling. I'd like to say that I don't think this is that full opportunity, and I'd like that opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, today is your opportunity, I'm afraid, and I'm happy to -- it looks as though there may be a break at some stage today, and I'm happy to hear further from you later on once you've digested this, but you -- you'll appreciate that if the Chamber remains uncertain about elements here, then it's likely that that order would require the indictment to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I hear the Court seeking some clarification one way or the other, and I -- as I said, I do seek the opportunity to do that before any formal ruling is made in the interest of hopefully reducing the amount of work for the parties and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic, we are looking at the motion which you filed alleging defects in the form of the indictment, and in particular the way in which the concept of joint criminal enterprise is addressed in the indictment referring to four related joint criminal enterprises. There -- as the result of considering the issue carefully, in light of the motion and the Prosecution response, it does appear to the Trial Chamber that there may be a lack of clarity in parts of this indictment. Mr. Tieger has been asked to try to assist us. He's done what he can for the moment, and I will give him an opportunity later on this afternoon if he wishes to amplify that. Is there anything that you wish to say on this matter at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship. I'm very satisfied with your understanding of this problem. There are two aspects to it. It seems to me that at times the OTP is taking my case as the last opportunity to introduce new international law norms, that is, for example, by lowering the threshold for mens rea and some other things, and the same applies to this issue of multiple joint criminal enterprises. This notion does not exist in any legal system. We know from American jurisprudence, who treat conspiracy or anti-mafia laws, one of the aspects is so the introduction of precedents and the second aspect is the OTP's attitude towards me. Apparently they're not quite sure about their indictment, and they're trying to inundate me with the material and to make this case more complex than it already is, and that if they miss the target once, they will try again and finally hit it if possible. What I said last time, that I was going to challenge everything, here we see the proof why I have to challenge all this. The OTP maintains as if there were no 50.000 soldiers in Sarajevo and that there were 70.000 Serb soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let me interrupt you. I'm concerned about the allegations in the indictment, not what your view of the facts may be. And I would like you to tell me if there's anything you want to say about the motion itself and the response that we've heard today from Mr. Tieger and also the written response of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say was that the opposite side is already in the area of meritum and merits. The things are not as they are depicted. Your full understanding of this construct, of this novel notion such as the multiple joint criminal enterprises, is quite obvious to me, and that was the reason that prompted me to file this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be -- just so that you're not misled by anything I've said, it may be that the Trial Chamber will accept the notion of there being a number of joint criminal enterprises. The issue that I've been raising is the relationship of each joint criminal enterprise to the other and to the crimes which are alleged in the indictment. That's not particularly a problem that you've raised in your challenge, but it -- it flows -- our anxiety about this point flows from the challenge that you've made. Now, I think you've probably said all that there is to be said on this, and we'll hear if Mr. Tieger has any further submission later this afternoon, and you will have an opportunity if you want to say any more at that stage. I'd like to move to the next of these motions now, and that is a motion in relation to protective measures. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, let me explain to you the problem that the Trial Chamber has with this. Protective measures appear to us to be measures designed to protect witnesses and victims. And when the -- a party seeks protective measures, the party is normally expected to justify them. There has to be a reason for them. And the obvious -- obviously the appropriate rule is Rule 75. On the other hand, there are circumstances in which states seek to protect material, and to that the rule that applies is Rule 70. And the criteria and the requirements are quite different, and indeed there may be no reason to justify or explain why a certain condition has been attached to material. However, if the party seeks to introduce that material into court as evidence, then the Court will have a say on whether the condition can continue to apply and the evidence be admitted, and the Court may well refuse to admit the evidence if the condition is inconsistent with the requirements of a fair trial. Now, it seems to the Trial Chamber that these two entirely separate concepts are confused in this motion, and the motion gives no real indication that the measures which you ask us to note as already in place were actually measures justified under Rule 75. Now, if they were, then this Chamber is bound to accept them. The additional measures that you seek appear on the face of it to have nothing to do with Rule 75. They appear to be measures designed to protect the material itself at the instance of the state provider, and that's something that is not an appropriate exercise of the power of the Chamber under Rule 75. Now, am I and my colleagues misunderstanding something here, or do you accept that there is confusion in this motion between the application of these two rules?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually see the key issue at -- legal issue here in this submission that the question is whether protective measures granted pursuant to Rule 70 fall within the province of Rule 75(F), such as the continued mutatis mutandis. And if they do, the Prosecution's notifications for protective measures of some of the witnesses - and I'm not going into the details because that would need to go into private session, I just stay on the legal issue as such - we think -- and we are actually supported by two decisions of this Tribunal, namely, one in the Martic case and one in the Prlic case, that 75(F) indeed does -- do apply also to all protective measures, no matter on what basis they were actually provided in the first proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are these decisions reasoned decisions in which the issue arose as a contested issue? Because it certainly has been determined in Milutinovic that this approach is wrong, and that was in a contested situation where the Trial Chamber had to address the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The decision I was actually referring to, the Martic decision, is of the 13th of January, 2006, where they actually said that the Rule 70 protective measures continue to apply, and they referred to 75(F); and the other decision is in the Prlic case of the 13th of April, 2006, with the same arguments basically. That's why -- we are aware -- we are aware of the Milutinovic decisions, but we think that what we actually argue is correct, and we would stay with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you refer to the Milutinovic decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But can you answer the question I posed: Was there opposition in Martic and Prlic to that course of action so that it was reasoned by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would have to check first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that Rule 75(F) says: "Once protective measures have been ordered in respect of a victim or witness in any proceedings ... such protective measures shall continue."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Rule 70 is nothing to do with victims or witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But we are talking actually about witnesses. We are not talking about materials. We are talking about protective measures for very particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Therefore, the argument actually would be that it falls under 75(F). And I would like to actually say why we think that's the case. If the purpose of Rule 75(F) is to expedite proceedings by allowing easy transfer of protective measures litigated before onto subsequent proceedings, I can't really see why that should be -- should not apply to any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The wording of the rule is clear. Now, you tell me that your application relates to victims and witnesses. For that submission to have any value, you would have to be seeking to protect the victims and witnesses and not the material. Are you telling me your application is designed to protect victims and witnesses and not to protect the material?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it's actually -- it's about the materials and the information that certain witnesses who were provided according to Rule 70 are providing then in court and -- no, that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we shall consider the authorities to which you are referring further in the light of this, we shall take account of what you say about the purpose and the purpose of construction of the Rules, and we shall make our decision. Mr. Karadzic, do you have anything to say on this issue? I understand that there was a delay in transmitting this motion to you in Serbian because of some confusion over the translation, but you may only have received it in the last day or so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact is that I'm no longer relieving -- receiving not only a transcript of testimony in B/C/S but also some other rulings. I -- most of the time I receive them in English which creates tremendous problems for me because I have to use the dictionary, and it's a time-consuming exercise. I appreciate your understanding again with regard to both the materials and the witnesses. Namely, if according to Rule 70 in any case consent was obtained from the country from which these documents originate, there is no need for me to apply for additional permit. That would be a discrimination against this case. If it is being granted in one particular instance, then it should be applied to this case as well. Before the OTP discloses either the material or the witness for whom certain measures are being requested, they should provide this consent; and after that, they should apply for the measures to be introduced. I think this is really important because this case is already gaining such a shape of high complexity, and it is really questionable how this trial is going to go on if it is going to go on at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate your pragmaticism, and I can see sense in what both you and Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff say about the application of measures from one case to another. The problem is that when you do that on the basis of an inaccurate assessment of the law, then you run into difficulties when there is a genuine dispute. It's all very well to do it when everyone's in agreement. But to set the proper course in a trial that may last for some time, it's important that we do so on a correct legal basis, and that's what the Trial Chamber intends to do. That doesn't mean to say that the same measures may not end up being applied. It also does not mean to say that the Chamber seeks to intervene in any way in the disclosure process. If conditions are imposed by a state on material, then these conditions have to be observed in the disclosure process without the Trial Chamber becoming involved. The Trial Chamber really only needs to be involved when that material is destined to be evidence and unusual conditions are sought to be applied to the way in which it's presented as evidence. However, as I said, we will look again at the various authorities referred to and the arguments presented, and we will issue a decision. The next one I want to deal with is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have wrongly assumed, Mr. Karadzic, that you had said all you want to say on the question of protective measures. It is your right to make a written submission if you wish, but if you've said enough on the matter, we can go ahead and deal with our decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add that so far it has not happened that the Defence disclose something that was protected. If in any case the measures are consented to by a government with the limitations of confidentiality, we're always ready to respect that, to respect the measures required by any government concerned and to respect confidentiality. But we don't believe we should be discriminated compared to other cases. If things were allowed in other cases, other trials, then it should be allowed here too. And if it need be, I will submit a written motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think that is unnecessary. Your point has been noted, and we will proceed on that basis that you have responded to this motion, and we will take account of your submissions in making our decision. I turn now to the motion to dismiss the indictment for abuse of process, and this relates to the searches which you raised at the last Status Conference. Now, when you got the Prosecution's response to your motion, you applied for leave to reply. You've done that a great deal in connection with various motions before the Trial Chamber. It's not necessary to reply to every response that you get from the Prosecution, and that's particularly so when you're simply repeating, as you have done from time to time, simply repeating and emphasizing the arguments you've already made. It's the exception rather than the rule for a reply to the presented, and it should be presented only to deal with something that has to be dealt with, and you haven't really foreseen it and dealt with it in the original motion. So you don't need to be afraid that because you haven't said something twice the Trial Chamber might think you don't really mean it. We'll always take account of every submission that you make. Now, in this case, is this Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff -- Mr. Tieger, I just want to be clear that what can be made available before we make our decision has been made available, and there is reference in your response to at the time of the seizure the MUP providing the resident of the premises - that's on the second search - with a list of items seized and then providing them with a copy of the search warrant and then providing your field office in Sarajevo with copies of the documents seized during the search. And you say once the materials are received in The Hague, you will discharge your disclosure obligations. Now, are you in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe we've received the -- all of the materials yet, and I need to clarify in addition if there's any misunderstanding about that, that the discharge of our disclosure obligations will be pursuant to the applicable jurisprudence and not dictated by the accused's view of what he should or should not receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate issue of course from the actual searches themselves, two separate matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My understanding is that we don't yet have the materials in-house, although I believe their receipt is imminent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's rather surprising that they should arrive in your office in Sarajevo on the 21st of April and be regarded as not urgent. We're now another - what? - more than two weeks down the line, and you still don't have them. I will always be concerned about what appears to be a lack of urgency in this case. But if that's the best you can tell me in the circumstances, then we shall proceed on that basis. Now, Mr. Karadzic, is there anything you wish to say further on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship. This is the first time that individuals whose flat has been searched and raided were able to see what was taken away. In the previous raid on the 2nd of December and the NATO raids, allegedly pursuant to instructions from this Tribunal, or rather, the OTP, my family and friends were taken to a different room while the search was going on, and they didn't know what goods were taken. So when on the 2nd of December they arrived at 3.00 a.m. to talk to my wife and ask her what she knew about Mladic, they took away an unidentified number of items, and there are two aspects in that regard. First of all, it impedes my defence because documents are being sought for which could be important to my defence which I will disclose if I find them; and secondly, it can discourage potential witnesses. They are being intimidated, and that is impermissible, and in my submission, that in any other country would be grounds for rejecting and dismissing the whole trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's only right that I should observe, Mr. Karadzic, that there's no evidence before the Tribunal that Prosecution in this case were in any way linked to the search on the 2nd of December, and that therefore the circumstances are rather different from those in a domestic jurisdiction, where if the police are involved, you can relate it to the Prosecution process in some way. But in the circumstances like this, in an International Tribunal where domestic authorities carry out searches and the International Tribunal authorities have no connection with these, then the same link cannot so readily be made. However, we will again take account of the various submissions that have been made before issuing our decision on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to add something? In all searchs so far the NATO porte-parole and international forces referred to this Tribunal, and since I've been here, that is to say the end of July last year, there are no further reasons for going to my family in search of documents. The documents that I come by and that some of my friends have, I will disclose in due course on time. And I think that you can check that torture -- and during the searchs that NATO was behind all the searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you are able to draw our attention to particular items which you say have been removed and that -- which you would otherwise have used, then you would be in a quite different situation from the one you've presented to us so far. So we will look at these circumstances as and when details are presented to the Trial Chamber. Now, I want to turn to the motion that you have made to reject the interim pre-trial brief, and this may be rather timely in ensuring that when the final pre-trial brief is presented, that it complies with the Rules. Now, at first glance, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, there is substance in the claim that you have used annexes to supplement the argument presented in the pre-trial brief. I note that you didn't use the full word limit extension which was granted, but it does look as though the annexes are simply supplementary, additional, argumentative material that you would normally expect to see in the pre-trial brief itself. Is that being unfair to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually saw it differently. As you can see, the annex -- Annex B looks sort of different from the Schedules A to G that we had included as well, but it's basically something very similar. It's a narrative of additional references to events, people, and institutions that you also find in these others. So it's -- Annex B is not really different from the others. What we wanted to do is we wanted to give as much information possible on -- and make references to people, to certain events, and institutions involved. So we didn't consider that to be argumentative, just more references. But of course if you consider this to be not within the margins of the direct -- Practice Direction, we would have to take consequences for the final pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me give you an example in relation to Bratunac. "On the 3rd of May, 1992, the Serb TO surrounded the Muslim village of Hranca and torched 43 houses. Over the following week they attacked and arrested the remaining residents of the village. A total of 12 Muslim villagers, four of whom had been captured, including one 6-year-old girl, were killed by Serb forces during the attack." Following that you then say: "More details on this incident are found at Schedule A, paragraph 3.1." In addition there are facts related to Schedule A, 3.2; and B, 4.1 in this municipality. Now, are you telling me that these are not simple factual statements that you expect to find in a pre-trial brief? Is that your serious submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually viewed it this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say -- what's it's a reference to? You say it's a reference. I mean, the Rule --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Reference to event, people, and institutions. For instance, we also added in the schedules A, B, and C we also added information in relation to perpetrators and institutions and categories that you didn't find in the original one. So I can't really see much of a difference between Annex B and the other schedules where we also added this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well that makes it worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's how we saw it, that it would be permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But read the Practice Direction. "An appendix will not contain legal or factual arguments, but rather references, source materials, items from the record, exhibits, and other relevant non-argumentative material." Now, are you seriously suggesting that the passage I've just read falls within that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we considered and we -- actually, when we produced Annex B, we actually were very careful not to make any argument related to the JCE or to responsibilities. That's how we saw it. But if you see it otherwise, I mean we can definitely with -- this can then be stricken, and we would then have to provide it with the final pre-trial brief and request a different word limit. If that's your view, we can definitely do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, you raised this issue, and you raised it purely and simply as a technical issue. You did not make a serious point about it. You asked that the Rules be observed, and you I think say -- actually say in the motion that you don't mind getting the information, but you think it should all be done properly within the Rules. Now, the Trial Chamber agrees with that view. The question is how to interpret the Rules and the Practice Direction and whether this is the right way to do it or whether it should be done differently. And we need to make that decision before the final pre-trial brief is due. We're not going to -- the Trial Chamber is not going to reject this one. It purpose is served now, anyway, in alerting us to this problem and alerting the Trial Chamber to other matters, but we are interested in hearing if you've anything else to say on the subject of the pre-trial brief that will be due on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have anything to add. I would just like to say that I agree, once again, to your view of the matter; and I'd also like to say that there's no need for things to be put in and slipped into annexes that could be disclosed to us otherwise and for them to think that we won't notice that. But we are opposed to having -- we're not opposed to having the length of the briefs increased. So I do allow for that. But of course that everything should be done according to the book, according to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just waiting for a copy of the brief to be brought in until I look at something that I need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have had this before me earlier. See, it boils down to you really saying that the crime base for the case can be put in an annex basically. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's true, and there are actually examples -- rather I would say for the final trial briefs where this is done because it's just such a huge case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, should we decide that that's not the correct way to do it and that the crime base should be part of the pre-trial brief and therefore count towards the word limit, what would your motion be?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We would then ask for an extension of the word limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To include actually the annexes counting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but do you know how similar your final version will be to this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In size?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think it will be slightly bigger because we want to expand in particular on the footnote references. We will add more reference -- evidence references in the body, and so therefore it necessarily will be bigger but not -- not hugely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I want to deal -- before we have the break, there's two things I'd like to deal with. The first is the motion to preclude reference to confidential decisions. Now, I think we're all in agreement on this one, that a method has to be found of ensuring that if reference is made to something confidential, that information is available to the opponent and available to the Trial Chamber. Having said in your response that you acknowledge that, and I suppose the same response is made to the other cases -- in the other cases where the same point has been raised, I think -- it's not just in this case, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it's only in this case, but we could check that. I'm not aware ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought the same motion may have been made in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, I misunderstood now. I thought you were referring to our own motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, in the Prlic case. Yes. In the Prlic case the decision was actually made that this is not proper and that the Prosecution should endeavour to produce public versions or redacted versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is that recent?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Relatively, yes, relatively, yes. And it's actually referred to in our response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But has Mr. Karadzic not made the same motion in other cases where he is seeking material from -- confidential material?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, okay. Well, in relation to this point, the problem that we have with your response is: How do you do it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will actually have to approach the Trial Chamber that dealt with this confidential decision and request a public version, that's one option; or to ask them to be -- to use this decision with redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, so you acknowledge that -- you acknowledge that you would not -- it would not be proper to refer to confidential decisions without making them available to the Bench and to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is there anything to be added to that, Mr. Karadzic? You seem to have achieved the objective.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's how I understood it. That's why we proposed it, because we can't guess at what they're aiming at if it's not disclosed. That's why we asked for disclosure. All of the confidential material from current trials and from previous trials. So there's no need to hide anything from us, all the more so as we are willing to respect the rules of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other matter I'd like to deal with quickly before we adjourn is the motions that have been made by both Prosecution and the accused for certification to appeal the decision on six preliminary motions challenging jurisdiction. Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution have applied for certification on one point, and that is the definition of the mens rea or mental-element standard for the third form of joint criminal enterprise, where the Chamber found that the correct test was one of probability rather than possibility. Do you have anything to say to oppose that motion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, I've noticed that the Trial Chamber on several occasions helped the OTP, correcting their mistakes and omissions. Now the Trial Chamber has made a good decision, taking into account our motion and request, and now the Prosecution are asking that that be deleted. That is something that should absolutely not be done, all the more so as the OTP has kept -- well, imagine this: If there were the possibility of somebody being injured at a football match, that you shouldn't organise football matches at all; or if there's a large construction -- a large building under construction, a worker is injured, that that building shouldn't be constructed. So this decision of the Trial Chamber is a good one, it's a good ruling, and they shouldn't be allowed to challenge it because I think that the OTP really did make big mistakes. And had it not been the Trial Chamber's indulgence in helping them out, matters would have been even worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Tieger, the -- or Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's not clear, the accused has applied for leave -- for certification to appeal the same decision in relation to four of the subjects dealt within it in which the Trial Chamber went on to consider whether what he had advanced was a challenge -- actually a challenge to the form of the indictment. There seems to be a bit of uncertainty in the motion because I think in relation to two of them the Trial Chamber did not in fact find that there was an issue in relation to the form of the indictment. Do you have any -- do you oppose his motion for certification?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would actually prefer, as we received it only this morning, we would actually prefer to respond to the issues in writing. We can only already forecast that we would oppose at least two of these, that's the -- the first one is the preliminary motion to dismiss Count 11 because we think that's actually a factual issue that we are talking about here that needs to be determined at trial, so therefore we would oppose certification. The same in relation to number 4, preliminary motion on lack of jurisdiction's superior responsibility, we also think that's just a factual matter to be determined at trial. In relation to the other two, lack of jurisdiction omission liability and also in relation to superior responsibility, we actually think that the issues raised have been previously decided on appeal already. So that -- we doubt that there is a reason that we can say that immediate resolution is necessary to advance the proceeding. So we tend to oppose all four, but that was only a preliminary screening of the -- of the request and the decision. So we would rather prefer to produce something in writing if that would assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I doubt if it will particularly. You may have said what is to be said on these matters, but I would be grateful if during the break you may give some further thought to any other submission you want to make on this because we are anxious that in view of the time that every appeal process takes in the interlocutory phase of the case, that these appeals are mounted if they are to be mounted very quickly. And there's bound to be an appeal on this decision anyway because the accused can appeal of right and -- as of right and has indicated his intention to do so. So we might as well as quickly as possible resolve the certification issues, too, so that they're all dealt with at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not persuaded by the accused's -- I can tell you, none of the Trial Chamber is persuaded by the accused's submission that we should delay a decision in certification until the appeals as of right are determined. That would simply result in an ultimate delay in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, definitely this will be what I just conveyed in relation to the four certifications applications. This will be our argument. Of course I just made it very briefly, and it would in writing of course be much more thorough and probably also with references to the decisions and jurisprudence here. But if -- if the Trial Chamber would not want any more argument on this and its sufficient what we said so far, then there's no need for me to elaborate on it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Mr. Karadzic, is there anything further you want to say on these motions for leave to appeal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about my submission for certification. You, yourself, could have noticed how urgent this is. There is a difference in dead-lines, seven days with regard to this Chamber and 15 days with regards to Appellate Chamber, and in that respect this should be granted as well as an extension of time so that we can coordinate our activities. I have to say that 35 pages of this ruling submitted only in English has taken up a lot of time for me to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll adjourn now for our break and resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me see now if we can dispose of some of the matters we've discussed so far. I've had the opportunity of meeting with the other Judges in the Chamber in the break and can now try to finalise some of these. The motion to reject the interim pre-trial brief, let's see if we can deal with this finally. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can you help me at all on the likely variation to the word count that you seek on the basis that we do not consider that the annexes are the appropriate place for crime base material?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Annex B or all annexes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything that you consider to be similar to Annex B in its content.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just heard from Mr. Reid that the Annex B is 18.000 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On its own?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's -- that would be Annex B. And as I said, Annex A, B, and C also has a -- additional information in there that goes past the -- the references to evidence because it states in a column, for instance, for the -- for the detention facilities it states who ran it, the authority who ran it. If you would consider that to be of that same character, that it wouldn't fit into the directives, then we would also have to have this A, B, and C -- Schedules A, B, and C added as well because they all have this information -- additional information, while the others don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does Mr. Reid know the total for all of these?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He is just checking.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For the Schedules A, B, and C it's 7.400 words, and I would think for the additional -- for the additional footnotes that we would have to add to the body of the pre-trial brief, I would think another 5.000 words perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will thought you said 18.000 for Schedule B --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, 18.000 for Schedule B and for the Schedules A, B, and C -- annex, sorry, I misspoke. Annex B, that's 18.000. But for the Schedules A, B, and C, which are a different annex -- Annex A, actually, that's another 7.400 words. And we would actually also need some more for the body of the pre-trial brief, the final version, and my rough estimate would be something -- maximum 5.000 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I shall authorise an increase in the word limit to 60.000 words for the purpose of the pre-trial brief. It's clear that the brief is designed to be helpful. We have already found it in many parts to be helpful. There's no point in wasting time in debating the exact figure in the light of the fact that we know the rough formation of this already and know that it's going to consume over 50.000, let's hope 60.000 is sufficient to cover it. I'm sure if you found that there was some modest further increase required, you would submit that along with the brief itself. If there's -- a real problem emerges, then we would expect earlier notice of the need for us to review the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, that I think sorts out the question of how to abide by the Rules and the Practice Direction to which you drew attention. Can I invite you now to consider whether the best course of action is for you to withdraw the motion that you previously made to reject the interim pre-trial brief since your objective has been achieved?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not opposed to this course of action. I can do it as well, and I can hopefully count on reciprocal generosity whenever I would require an excessive number of words or more words than allowed, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shall permit you to withdraw the motion. I turn now to the motion to preclude reference to confidential decisions. The Trial Chamber has noted that the objective of that has also been achieved, and therefore we deny that motion as unnecessary, not on its merits but as in the circumstances now unnecessary. The other thing that we discussed was the motion for certification to appeal. We note that Mr. Karadzic has indicated his intention to exercise his right to appeal in relation to the question of whether these motions were truly challenges to jurisdiction. So far as the issues for which certification is sought, dealing first of all with his motion, we grant certification in relation to the motion to dismiss Count 11 for lack of jurisdiction since we consider both legs of the test for certification are met. We refuse certification in relation to the other three. The second leg of the test is not met in relation to the second one, that's omission liability which is a very fact-intensive issue in any event, and there is already substantial jurisprudence on it. So far as the other two are concerned, special intent crimes and superior responsibility, the Chamber did not address these as challenges to the form of the indictment. There is no issue that we can identify on which we could grant certification. We do not consider that either leg of the test has been met in relation to these, and we accordingly deny certification. So far as the issue raised by the Prosecution is concerned, that is the mental element test for foreseeability in relation to the third form of joint criminal enterprise, we consider that both legs of the test for that are met, and we grant certification to appeal that decision. There has yet to be determined the date on which the proposed amended indictment should be filed. We will state a date in the decision we issue dealing with the other two remaining challenges to the form of the indictment, so you need take no action on the amended indictment until you get that decision. Now, Mr. Karadzic, the next motion to which I want to turn is your motion for equality of arms in contact with the news media. I just want to be sure that there is nothing further you have to say on this matter before it is finally dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me just briefly to say that I am disappointed with your ruling. If we look at the Blaskic case, which is much older than the Kvocka case, the case law of this Court has been quite different and the OTP is relying on it; however, the situation is as it is. There's nothing to be done about it. So I will leave it up to the Appeals Chamber to decide whether this appeals can be filed and if it refers to jurisdiction. As far as the relations with media is concerned, I am appearing here as my own Defence counsel, not as an accused. Therefore, the same means and the same limitations should be equally applied to both the Defence and the accused. I have to tell you that the degree of demonisation of someone is so great that any acquittal is impossible. If I work on a daily basis, it is impossible for me to refute everything that the OTP has done in terms of demonising me and the Serbian people. In order to do that, I would have to be allowed to speak to the media almost on a daily basis in order to redress and rectify the damage that we have incurred. You are taking due care of the fairness of the trial, and therefore you should take an appropriate position regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber has carefully considered this, and we are entirely satisfied it does not raise an issue of equality of arms in the pre-trial or, indeed, in the trial and raises no question relating to the fairness of the trial, whatever else it may raise. Indeed, so far as the trial and pre-trial processes are concerned, your motion borders on the frivolous. The Chamber therefore denies the motion. We also suggest to you that your time would be far better spent concentrating on the issues which are genuine issues in the case. For what it's worth, I read about you regularly in press reports more than once a day; that may be no consolation, but it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, that is -- I'm not concerned about what conclusion you're going to arrive at; however, in view of the fact that we are expecting to hear 490 witnesses in this courtroom and someone really has to strike a balance regarding the influence on these 490 witnesses. I'm not so concerned about the expert witnesses, but these 490 witnesses will come here coached and full of prejudices. And this is what -- this is going to be the doing of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can rest assured that the Judges here are well able to ensure in the course of a trial that nothing unfair arises. Your motion does not raise anything that has an impact on the fairness of the process at the moment or indeed the trial process in due course. That takes me now to the motion for further extension of time and ancillary orders in relation to the motion you want to make about immunity from prosecution. Now, this is a developing situation as I understand it, and you have been provided with material from one state in the last few days. There are ongoing discussion about that material, but it may be that that's as much as you are going to have immediately to hand from that source for the purpose of this motion at present. Maybe, that's all I can say. You also seek information from another state, and you have complained about their failure to respond. That has concerned us, and we have done our best to clarify the position, and you'll appreciate that I'm referring in this connection to the state of Sweden. And I'm now informed that the earliest at which a response to your request may be anticipated is the beginning of next week. There will be a time fairly soon where this motion has to be tendered in its final form so that we can start the adjudication process. That does not stop you making changes to that motion if and when you obtain further information if that happens. But we're getting to the stage where the dead-line is going to have to be met. And I'm inclined at the moment to indicate to you that this motion should be submitted in 14 days' time. Now, in light of that view, is there anything further you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, I was delighted to hear from the US government that they would do their best to arrive at the truth, and we indeed received some documents, and we are currently seeking consent from their government approval to use them. I also hope that the Swedish government will facilitate an interview with their minister. We're also going to ask from other governments, Germany and others, very sensitive and numerous documents. If they are delaying things on such a rather benign matter as this one, I wonder what is going to happen if some more serious issues arise. I would like to say that on a daily basis with tremendous delays, though, we are obtaining documents that are going to be needed. Only I didn't understand your dead-line of 14 days. What specifically did you have in mind compared to what was said before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've asked for an extension of time to submit your motion. My understanding is that you want to withdraw the motion you originally made way back the very first day you were here and submit a more detailed motion in light of the up-to-date position. We've got to set a dead-line for that because then the Prosecution have to have time to respond. We've got to have time to consider it. It may be a serious enough issue to have a hearing for all we know, and that's something that you've suggested already. So all of that will take time, and time is marching on. So we need to get the thing going, and it seems to me that 14 days is about as much as you can now be given in addition to what you've had so far to start the process, on the basis that if more information comes to light you will be permitted within reason to tender that information and to alter your position in the light of it, make the case more precise or whatever. But what I'm suggesting is that it might be reasonable now to give you another 14 days on the basis that you use what you do have to submit the motion so the Prosecution can see the general tone of this motion and begin their own preparations to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for these 14 days that will start running from today or tomorrow, I suppose. But I would also kindly ask the Trial Chamber, provided these governments fail to provide these materials, that the Trial Chamber obligates them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well at the moment I don't think it's appropriate to make an order to that effect. What I shall do is make an order that your motion in relation to immunity from prosecution must be submitted no later than the 25th of May. Now, that gives you more than two weeks, and it takes you over a weekend as well. So it's the maximum of time I think it's reasonable to give you. The Prosecution will have the normal 14 days to answer that. There's -- that's one that the time will not be cut down on because I think time could be valuable for both of you. The -- there was another dead-line I had in mind, and it's gone from my mind. Oh, yes. The motion that you have submitted for extension includes a request for orders for additional information. Now, I'm not suggesting that this is a very precise motion at the moment, but it does identify the -- two of the sources from which you seek information. And you rightly make the point that it may be appropriate to consider whether you need an order to get information. So this will be -- the consideration of this motion will be continued, and it will remain on the agenda of the Status Conference. And the next Status Conference will be probably on the 3rd of June. So on the afternoon of the 3rd of June, this should be on the agenda. And hopefully the information you have required will have been received. If in the interim there is other information that you consider is not being provided but should be provided, then obviously you should notify the Trial Chamber in advance of the 3rd of June, long enough in advance for us to be able to decide what measures are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps I can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have asked you for any comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Actually what we were -- we were actually in the process of opposing the motion of extension of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- for the following reason, and I also would suggest that everybody considers it. It would actually be at this point in time, we are spending a lot of time and resources, in particular also the accused, resources on the issue pursuing factual issues in relation to the Holbrooke Agreement, and we actually think it should be time to determine the legal issues first. The accused could, for instance, file a preliminary motion setting out his legal arguments in accordance with the dead-line issued by the Trial Chamber based on an assumed set of facts. That's actually a position that was taken in a case here already at the Tribunal, and that is the Dragan Nikolic case. The accused in that case challenged the Tribunal's jurisdiction based on an alleged illegal arrest. The Trial Chamber in that case first determined the legal issues based on a set of assumed facts, and having determined this legal issue then -- then it would have turned to the factual issues, if they at all would matter. Let's say if we would -- if the accused would file a motion setting out the alleged facts and we would -- it would be assumed as being the basis, and then the legal issue could be decided. I do actually have this decision here in the Nikolic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're pushing at an open door, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. I agree entirely with your submission, and I think it's inevitable that the matter will have to be dealt with that way if the accused continues to have difficulty in recovering material which he thinks exist but about which there may be some doubt. So I'm happy -- but -- to make that suggestion, but again it's going to take time to put this together, and I think that time may also result in the provision of additional factual information. So I'm not inclined to depart from the time-scale envisaged because I don't think it's interfering with the preparations for the trial in a serious way. Even if we cut the time down, I suspect it will continue throughout the period until a decision is made to be a running issue, a running sore, as it were, but not one which will directly interfere with the preparations necessary for the trial.
