Mr. Karadzic, what's been suggested is very sensible, that when you submit your motion, you should, even in the absence of specific factual information which you seek, assume that you're going to get the information that you think exists and advance your legal case on that assumption. That will enable the Trial Chamber, if it cannot address the whole situation based on a clear factual position, nevertheless to address the legal question that you raise assuming you can prove the facts. So please address it that way, and that will ensure that this motion that you will now present will be one which deals fully with the issue of immunity. I do not change the indication I've given about the date for you to submit the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of May; is that right? In this motion I'm going to include what you have just requested, and that is the accessible documents. And I'm grateful for the opportunity to include the documents that would arrive subsequently, that is to say after that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. But please also bear in mind the suggestion that you assume that you will get them and make your argument accordingly so that the whole position is clear when you submit the -- at least the whole argument that you wish to present is clear when you submit the motion. That I think completes what we have to deal with except the matter that I asked Mr. Tieger to reflect upon during the break, which is the terms of the indictment relating to the various joint criminal enterprises. Now, if you like, there -- I can go through further passages to explain the predicament if that's going to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It -- I have no objection to that, of course, Your Honour. I was going to do -- I was going to take a page from the Court's book and do the converse and point the Court to what I thought addressed the concern raised in a clear manner. For example, I was going to address the Court's concern that Counts 4, 5, and 6 related only to the overarching joint criminal enterprise and point to the portions of the indictment that indicate the contrary, but I'm more than happy to proceed in whatever manner the Court thinks more suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you understood me as saying Counts 4, 5, and 6 only related to the overarching joint criminal enterprise, then you misunderstood me because that is one situation where it clearly isn't confined to that, as paragraph 62 makes clear. But if I can just very quickly do this with you, Mr. Tieger. Look at paragraph 37 which relates to Count 1, genocide, and we'll go through these count by count. You'll see that in paragraph 37 it's made clear that it's the overarching joint criminal enterprise that is being pled in relation to commission of genocide under Count 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The relation -- the reference to paragraphs 9 through 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you look at Count 2 and paragraph 42, you'll see there that the reference is to the third joint criminal enterprise and is confined to that third joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And as we discussed earlier, there is also reference to JCE 3, and I think it's in paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that is Count 2. Then if you go to Count 3 and paragraph 50, and the count is persecutions, you'll see there that the reference is to the first overarching joint criminal enterprise. And then if you go to Counts 4, 5, and 6, paragraph 62, you'll see there that the reference is to the overarching one and two of the other joint criminal enterprises. Now, all of that I think fits so far with what you are suggesting. And then Counts 7 and 8, you'll see at paragraph 70 that the murder and extermination charges commission is confined apparently to the first joint criminal enterprise. And then when we get to Counts 9 and 10 in paragraph 77 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Your Honour, for the record I think you said murder and extermination, I believe you meant deportation and inhumane acts for 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, 4, 5, and 6 are murder and extermination. Then 7 and 8, sorry, deportation and inhumane acts, and they are apparently confined as far as commission is concerned to the first joint criminal enterprise. Then 9 and 10, terror and unlawful acts, paragraph 77, you'll see that that's the second of the averred joint criminal enterprise. And no reference here to the first one at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then in Count 11 the third -- sorry -- well, the fourth, the third of the other joint criminal enterprises is referred to in paragraph 84. And no reference again to the overarching joint criminal enterprise. Now, you're quite clear that that's what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact I think the Court -- I'm a little confused at this point about where the -- we depart in our understanding of the indictment. The Court expressly referred to a number of counts as it proceeded in its recitation where -- that it found to be consistent with the position earlier articulated by the Prosecution. I think I now understand you to be saying that we find ourselves in the end at odds with the Court's view that there's a problem in the way -- in the averments here. It -- to the extent that we've articulated the nature of the objectives of -- and nature of the JCEs today and in the interim pre-trial brief, as I mentioned before, yes, I think the indictment is consistent with that and is an expression of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to illustrate the problem. If the accused was right that there's no basis for having multiple joint criminal enterprises in an indictment like this and the three other joint criminal enterprises were struck down, for charges Counts 9, 10, and 11 you would -- your case would be confined to the forms of liability other than commission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've alleged -- we've alleged clearly a large number of crimes in this indictment. Again, I'll turn to Counts 4, 5, and 6 because I think they offer a great deal of clarity. Those were committed, as the indictment alleges, in a variety of ways, through various -- various modes of liability. Commission through three discrete and separate joint criminal enterprises, for -- pursued with different objectives in mind but related objectives, as we've also articulated, through planning, ordering, et cetera. Those are all expressly identified in the indictment. Now, one thing we -- and if the Court were inclined to find some flaw in the -- in this indictment, it certainly could not be that we did not allege these crimes and did not allege that they were committed through all the modes of liability, planning, ordering, instigating, and committing, plus aiding and abetting. So I would reject that. But one thing we haven't discussed, Your Honour, while we've been talking about to some extent the relationship between the JCEs, the extent to which they overlap, interrelate, we haven't talked about the accused's notion that charging focused modes of liability via separate JCEs is some kind of problem analogous to the problem of multiple conspiracies in a jurisdiction like the United States --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have a problem with that one, Mr. Tieger. That's why I haven't raised it with you. That's another -- that's quite a separate issue. All I wanted to do is ensure that you have had an opportunity to consider whether you've set out these -- the link between these joint criminal enterprises to your own satisfaction. And you're quite clear that nothing has been omitted here, then we will proceed to deal with the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would -- again, I mean, I don't know if I mentioned this at the outset, but I'm very grateful for the opportunity to re-address the Court and appreciate the Court's in that regard. So maybe I'm grabbing at too much here, but I would like an opportunity to review today's record and, if possible, submit something in writing to the Court by tomorrow if there is something that needs to be added. I obviously tried to articulate the relationship between these JCEs, the nature of the overarching JCEs, the fact that the discrete JCEs further the objective of the overarching JCE and are quite sufficiently related to it. And all -- and what they primarily accomplish is to add greater focus and specificity to this indictment. But again, I'd be pleased for the opportunity to see if there is something that we have been discussing here that I have failed to properly address to the Court, and they could provide the Court with additional illumination before it renders any ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, do you want to say any more on this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, thank you. Well, not only is it the practice of other national legislations, American's and others, but the practice of this court as well. There are some 50 cases at this Tribunal and never has this multiple criminal enterprise, joint criminal enterprise occurred. And I think that this is going to complicate something that's already very complicated and a voluminous case. And on the other hand, I'm wasting a lot of time here because we might receive the fourth amended indictment only at the end of the year. And I'm sure that this Pre-Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber will recognise and adhere to all my requests. And it would be much better if the Prosecution were to accept your well-intentioned proposals, Your Lordship, and amend the indictment in the space of a few weeks, not to have it arrive in December because then these whole proceedings will be extended a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just one quick point of clarification. I guess it's the second time, mentioned in the motion, the accused just mentioned that the representation that multiple JCEs in a case is unprecedented. That's not the case, as the Court is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not going to assist the Trial Chamber to engage in another round of written submissions because that is effectively what you're asking, Mr. Tieger. I think adequate opportunity has been given to both sides to state their position to us, and my colleagues and I will consider what's been said today and take that into account with the other submissions and make a determination of the motion, and that will be fairly soon; it may even be this week. If it's not this week, it will certainly be next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is there any other matter you wish to raise? That exhausts my agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are a number of motions that are waiting, but I don't want to broach that topic today until the time is ripe to do that. But I would like to say -- raise some general matters. What regularly happens, as Your Lordship rightly anticipated, that I would be inundated with a vast number of documents and papers, and unfortunately that is what is happening. And usually on the day of the Status Conference itself or on the eve of the conference. Now, I need my associates, my legal advisors pro bono and others, those who had been appointed by the Registry, and they are in Australia, New Zealand, The Hague, New York, London, so how can I contact them just one day before the Status Conference and get through all that material and be ready for the Status Conference? So what I wanted to say is this: It seems that the material is being disclosed to me at the 11th hour, and I don't receive the documents in Serbian. So I do need to receive all this material in Serbian. Furthermore, I'm afraid that I'll have to make other requests of the Trial Chamber, that is, to provide me -- that the Court provide me with a laptop. I'm very cooperative, and I have accepted electronic -- the electronic form. I'm not asking for hard copies, but I can't appear here and spend time searching through all my papers because I don't have the right to use a laptop in the courtroom, or rather, in my room so that I can prepare all the material to have it easily accessible and then to be able to present it to you here in court. So I would like to have this laptop in my room. I don't need to have any other connections, modems or whatever, but I think some rules are completely incomprehensible and detrimental to me, and that is one of them, the lack of a laptop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's not be too critical of either the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution for inundating you with material or for doing things at the last minute. You've fairly successfully inundated us with loads of material over the past few weeks, and your reference to a number of motions suggests that you've got the more in the offing. The question of the laptop comes out of the blue, of course, and that's something on which I'm just not in a position to comment because there may well be a good reason why you can't have a laptop in your room. All I can say to you is that I will find out for my own satisfaction what the position is. As far as things happening too quickly immediately before the Status Conference is concerned, that's inevitable. That's what this process is about. The idea of having a Status Conference is to provoke everyone into action just in case they haven't been as active as they should be. So that's going to happen at every Status Conference. I can't do anything about it. In fact, I'll be the first to encourage that degree of activity. So I'm afraid you'll need to get the passports out and bring the -- your supporters on the pro bono staff from Australia or wherever if you want to make full use of the opportunity that every Status Conference raises. You know perfectly well to what I'm referring. You have chosen this way. We do our best to satisfy the requirements that go with your chosen method of representation. We'll continue to do that. There are limits as you know. I note what you say, and anything that can be done to assist the exchange of information will be done. Mr. Tieger, is there anything that the Prosecution wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will have something, Your Honour, and if I can at the -- I mean, if I can revisit something quickly. I just wanted to clarify something in terms of the submission I made earlier. I was looking at the Court's comments. With respect to Count 3 and in reference to paragraph 50, perhaps this will be helpful for the Court, you indicated that that referred only to the first overarching criminal enterprise, Count 50, perhaps, but Count 3 refers to both -- as you continue on and begin at paragraph 57, you'll see the reference to Srebrenica, and I believe the same thing is true with Counts 7 and 8 where you will also see references to the Srebrenica JCE. The only other thing I'd like to add or to emphasize, to the extent it may be helpful, is that the -- there are different -- the different crime base and different incidents fall within the different JCEs. They are not -- the same crimes are not alleged as having been committed through different commission modes of liability through different JCEs. That may have been very clear; it may not have been part of the Court's problem, but I felt it necessary to emphasize that in case there was any concern that that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm having to re-read the transcript on what you've just said at the very end, Mr. Tieger. I don't think I follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was concerned on the basis of a couple of comments perhaps that I misunderstood, that there may be some misimpression that we find different underlying crimes, such as different individual acts of murder alleged to have been committed through more than one -- as an objective of more than one JCE, for example, that is not alleged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how do you then -- yeah. So paragraph 62 which is the most obvious example, if not the only example, you're saying that insofar as there are three separate commission vehicles in there or commission modes of liability they relate to different murders?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or I would kind of look at it the other way around, I guess. If you're looking at the individual murder and trying to understand the criminal responsibility, it arises from different JCEs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you now focus very clearly with that submission exactly the point that the accused is trying to make. Anyway, thank you very much. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one issue that I would like to raise in relation to the Work-Plan. We are all on track in relation to the dead-lines given. We will submit the witness list and the exhibit list and the final trial brief on the 18th of May. We can make that. However, we have one problem. In relation to paragraph 7.3 of the order of the 6th of April, and this paragraph says the following: "The list shall indicate with respect to each witness the exhibits which will be referred to in the course of the evidence of the witnesses," likewise, it says also, "with respect to each exhibit which witnesses will refer to the exhibits in evidence." The lists that we will provide on the 18th of March [sic] will include a reference to the tendering witness for almost all the exhibits except for bar table motions and these kind of exceptions. However, there's a factual reason that we are not able to provide the -- in relation to each and every exhibit information as to which witness would refer to them, different from tendering witness. This information depends on a variety of future actions and factors. For instance, whether a 92 bis or 92 quater motion is granted or whether a Rule 94(B) motion is granted or whether a tendering document through bar table is granted or finally also when a witness that we have planned to discuss an exhibit with and who would tender it then, if that witness becomes unavailable, then we really would have a problem and we -- if we have to make our final decision on all these things on the 18th of May. And finally there is also a logistical problem. We have very tight dead-lines, but we manage to meet them. But the witness list and the exhibit lists are currently being prepared and worked on by two different groups of people within our team. And they will work on their projects definitely until the 18th of May. To consolidate and actually bring all this information together so that we can say which witness would even speak about a certain exhibit, we just can't make that on the 18th of May for these logistical reasons, and also it's not practical, as I said before. So that is something that I just want to raise, that this is actually upcoming, and we may request an extension of time to facilitate this particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I reject your first submission that there are any practical difficulties associated with this. What the Tribunal -- what the Chamber expects is an indication of the possibility that a witness and a document or exhibit will be common. So any witness that might speak to this document should be named along with the document, and any document that a witness might speak to should be listed. 92 bis and other applications can't be dealt with at this stage, but the accused is entitled to the implementation of this order to ensure that we facilitate proper preparation of the Defence in the case. So I reject that. Your logistical point I'm most sympathetic to. If that does cause an insurmountable difficulty, then I'm sure that the Chamber will be flexible within reason to a certain degree. For example, recognising that the date for copies of the exhibits to be actually produced is later than the date for the list might allow for some flexibility, but I'm not prepared to modify the order in relation to the content of these lists. Now, if that creates another problem and you have to tender a written motion for further time, then you should do so. But please do not think that the Chamber will be sympathetic to deleting or not requiring some of the information listed here. And indeed I ought to make it clear to you now and the accused that there will be a further order pronounced in due course about the content of the Defence pre-trial brief, which will make demands on him. And in order to enable us to make proper demands on him for clarity that will assist you and us, then it will be our intention to secure implementation as far as possible of the orders we've already made about the lists required from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be allowed to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a little concerned about the efforts made by the Prosecution to ensure in such a hasty way this troubling methodology with respect to exhibits, testimony, and so on and so forth. We would like to ask that we be completely and fully informed. So that we can design our defence strategy, I must know everything about the witnesses and the topics that are going to be discussed. That's one matter. The other matter is that I can say that I'm satisfied with our method of work, and I would have been more satisfied had I been granted 6.000 more words, as the other side was, for the motion with respect to Holbrooke. You granted 6.000 words thus far, but it would be much easier to write the motion if I were to be allowed 12.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 6.000 was a very carefully considered figure in light of the issues. I don't think it's going to help you, Mr. Karadzic, or us or the Prosecution for that order to be varied. The point you wish to make is divided into two parts, and 6.000 is, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, sufficient to enable you to succinctly make your point. So please comply with that requirement. That completes the work of this Status Conference, and the court is now adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. My apologies for this. Only just to clarify one final point. Ms. Gustafson advises me that the manner in which I responded to the Court's final inquiry suggested that you could have one individual act of murder, one individual crime arising from multiple JCEs. That's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you said the opposite -- no, I didn't read you as saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.12 p.m.
